At ten, Preeti dropped her maths paper on the table. "Sir gave me low marks because he was in a bad mood. Some days it's just luck." Her maths teacher Tarun, passing the door, said only, "Show me which sums you practised." She looked at her shoes. She had practised none.

At fifteen, Preeti missed a scholarship list by three marks. That evening her father Imran lit a lamp and said quietly, "What is written is written, beta. It gives me some peace." Preeti nodded. In their home, faith in destiny was as ordinary as the morning prayer. But the next morning she opened her chemistry notes at six o'clock and said, "And I still have to do my part." Imran smiled and put a cup of tea beside her book.

She did not see any contradiction. The loss felt lighter because she believed something larger was at work, and the next exam was still hers to prepare for.

qa.q: How many marks did Preeti miss the scholarship list by?
qa.a: Preeti missed the list by three marks.

qa.q: How does Preeti's explanation for results at ten differ from her view at fifteen?
qa.a: At ten she blames luck and the teacher's mood and had practised none of the sums, while at fifteen she holds faith in destiny alongside her own effort, finding peace after the loss and still preparing for the next exam.

qa.q: What was Preeti probably feeling when she looked at her shoes after Tarun asked which sums she practised?
qa.a: Preeti felt caught out and a little ashamed, because she knew she had not practised any.

qa.q: What did Imran do that supported Preeti at fifteen?
qa.a: Imran shared his sense of peace about what is written, then supported her effort by putting a cup of tea beside her book the next morning.

grounding: Locus of control across two ages: a child who blames luck and the teacher's mood, and a teenager from a traditional home who holds faith in destiny together with hard effort.

Zainab's report card lay on the kitchen table, and she pushed it away. "Ms Fernandes gave me a low mark because she doesn't like me," she said. "The test was unfair. It's just my bad luck." She said the same thing about the spelling test, the drawing test and the sports day races. Each time her mother Disha, distracted by work calls, said, "We'll see," and moved on. Zainab stopped bringing up her results at all.

At school, the class teacher Jatin noticed that Zainab never tried the extra questions. "Why bother?" she said. "It happens or it doesn't." Jatin did not argue. He asked her to pick just five spelling words, practise them for a week and compare her score. Zainab got four out of five. She stared at the page as if it belonged to someone else.

That evening she said to Disha, quietly, "I practised, and it worked." Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through.

qa.q: How many of the five spelling words did Zainab get right?
qa.a: Zainab got four of the five words right.

qa.q: What connects Zainab's blaming of luck and teachers with her result on the five spelling words?
qa.a: Zainab says the low mark is bad luck and the test unfair, and skips the extra questions because it happens or it doesn't; after practising five spelling words she gets four out of five and says she practised and it worked. The small win shows her effort has an effect.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she said "Why bother?" to Jatin?
qa.a: Zainab felt discouraged and powerless, as if results simply happen to her.

qa.q: What did Disha do that helped Zainab?
qa.a: Disha put down her phone and listened all the way through, so Zainab felt heard instead of brushed off with "We'll see".

grounding: External locus of control in a child who blames luck, teachers and tests, and a small win that shows her effort has impact.

passage:
At nine, Divyansh slid a maths test with a red 8 under his pillow. His father Vijay had a single question at dinner: "What was your score?" When it wasn't full marks, he said nothing and went out to the balcony. Divyansh concluded that good marks meant love, and that mistakes were best kept out of sight.

At twenty-one, Divyansh sat in front of an internship form with the closing date on Friday. The résumé needed one more line, the cover letter one more polish, and the photo was slightly off. He told himself he would submit tomorrow when everything was ready. Friday came and went. So did the next form. His friend Bhavna asked, "Did you send it?" and Divyansh said, "Almost." He felt relief and dread at the same time. Doing nothing felt safer than sending something imperfect, and yet it meant the one outcome he feared.

That weekend, Bhavna sat beside him. "Send it rough," she said. "I'll sit right here." He winced, but he sent the next application at eleven at night.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Divyansh at dinner?
qa.a: Vijay asked, "What was your score?"

qa.q: How does the atmosphere at home when Divyansh is nine connect to his missed deadlines at twenty-one?
qa.a: At nine Divyansh learns from Vijay that marks bring warmth and mistakes are best hidden, and at twenty-one the same fear keeps him polishing forms until the deadlines pass, because doing nothing feels safer than sending anything imperfect.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he told Bhavna the form was almost sent?
qa.a: Divyansh felt relief and dread at once, afraid of sending something imperfect but also aware that the deadline had passed.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped Divyansh act?
qa.a: Bhavna encouraged him to send it rough and offered to sit with him, which made the risk of an imperfect application easier to take.

grounding: Perfectionism linked across ages: a child learning that love follows marks, and the young adult who lets deadlines pass because nothing feels ready.

On a wet afternoon, five-year-old Kalyani leaned on the table and sighed, "I'm bored. I want the video." Her father Uday put a tray of dried beans, glue and cardboard in front of her. "See what you can make." She sighed again, then began gluing beans into a face with a very wide mouth.

Four years later, Uday gave Kalyani a craft kit for her birthday, and she started with enormous excitement. She laid out the beads, sorted them by colour and made three bracelets on the first day. A week later, she also began a diary, writing two pages every night for four days. Then the beads sat untouched in their box and the diary lay under her pillow with a bent corner.

"It got boring in the middle," she told her teacher Vidya, who asked about the kit. Vidya smiled. "That flat middle is the hardest part. What if you make just one more bracelet, for a friend?" Kalyani took out the beads that weekend.

qa.q: What did Uday put in front of Kalyani when she said she was bored?
qa.a: Uday put a tray of dried beans, glue and cardboard in front of her.

qa.q: How does Kalyani's boredom at five relate to what happens with the craft kit and diary at nine?
qa.a: At five Kalyani sighs that she is bored and Uday gives her beans, glue and cardboard, so the boredom passes; at nine she starts the craft kit and diary with excitement but stops when the middle gets boring. The joy is in beginning, and tolerating the flat middle is still developing.

qa.q: What was Kalyani probably feeling when she told Vidya it got boring in the middle?
qa.a: Kalyani felt flat and bored once the excitement faded, and perhaps a little disappointed in herself for stopping.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped Kalyani?
qa.a: Vidya said the flat middle is the hardest part and suggested one more bracelet for a friend, a small step with a purpose.

grounding: Boredom in a young child answered by simple materials, and the same child later starting with excitement and abandoning the flat middle of a project.

At ten, Manjula told her teacher that the low mark was because the examiner was in a bad mood. "It's nothing to do with me," she said, and she rarely looked at her own mistakes. The habit lingered longer than she knew.

At twenty, she sat in the hostel canteen with two friends after their group project had gone badly. Deepika put her head in her hands. "It was all my fault. I should have checked everyone's part. I ruined it for the whole team." Anirban slammed his cup down. "Nobody helped me. The professor was unfair and the team was useless. I did nothing wrong."

Manjula listened. She heard herself at ten in Anirban's voice, and in Deepika she heard someone carrying weight that was not hers. "Let's list who did what," she said. "Deepika, you handled the slides; the data was late for reasons outside you. Anirban, the report's conclusion was rushed, and that part was yours." Both were quiet for a moment, then Deepika sat up. Anirban rubbed his neck and said, "Okay. That's fair."

qa.q: Where did Manjula sit with her two friends at twenty?
qa.a: Manjula sat in the hostel canteen.

qa.q: How does Manjula's own childhood view connect to what she sees in Deepika and Anirban?
qa.a: At ten Manjula blames the examiner and never looks at her own mistakes, like Anirban blaming everyone else at twenty, while Deepika takes on guilt for things she did not do; both distort, and Manjula separates each person's own part from circumstances.

qa.q: What was Deepika probably feeling when she said it was all her fault?
qa.a: Deepika felt guilty and overwhelmed, taking the blame for everyone's part in the project.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that helped both friends?
qa.a: She asked them to list who did what and gave each a fair share of the responsibility, which helped both see a balanced picture.

grounding: Locus of control seen in one person's childhood habit of blaming outside factors and in two young adults who overblame themselves or others.

At five, Tanvir slid off his chair and announced, "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His mother handed him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes. "Build something." He grumbled, then taped a very long telescope and spent the afternoon spotting imaginary ships.

At nine, Tanvir sat at the back of the classroom with his chin in his hand and his body sunk low in the chair. The teacher, also named Payal, saw it and thought, "He looks bored." She stopped beside his desk. "Tanvir, are you with us? Tell me what you're working on." He straightened a little. "I stayed up late finishing my model. And I was thinking about the answer. I think it's twelve." He was right.

His friend Hrithik whispered after class, "I thought you were asleep." Tanvir grinned. "I think better slumped." The teacher smiled and added, "Next time I'll ask first and assume later."

qa.q: What did Tanvir's mother give him when he said he was bored at five?
qa.a: She gave him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes.

qa.q: How do Tanvir's boredom at five and his slouching at nine differ in what they show?
qa.a: At five Tanvir's boredom is real and settled by simple materials, while at nine his slumped posture looks like boredom to the teacher but actually comes from tiredness and thinking, so posture is a clue and not proof.

qa.q: What was Tanvir probably feeling when he said he was thinking about the answer?
qa.a: Tanvir felt sleepy but engaged, comfortable slumped in a way that helped him think.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that was wiser than assuming?
qa.a: The teacher stopped at his desk and asked him about his work instead of deciding from his posture that he was bored.

grounding: Boredom in a young child answered by simple materials, and posture in school that looks like boredom but may mean tiredness or thinking.
